bug_description.original: OSS-Fuzz issue 42505804 (flatbuffers): Heap-buffer-overflow READ 1 found by fuzz target monster_fuzzer [asan]. https://issues.oss-fuzz.com/issues/42505804
bug_description.original_source: sample_info.json, reproduction_report.json, sanitizer_trace.txt, default_crash_trace.txt, patch.diff, the staged `poc`, and the staged vulnerable source under `gt_results/arvo_42505804/_work/src/flatbuffers`
bug_description.normalized: Stage 01's reproduced `monster_fuzzer` run parses the staged 305-byte witness as a Monster object whose `flex` field is a nested FlexBuffer string vector. After the harness strips the leading `0x20 0x20` bytes, `allow_non_utf8` is enabled and `ParseFlexBufferValue()` materializes two attacker-controlled strings: the first is 20 bytes long, and the second is 256 bytes long, begins with the same 20-byte prefix, and contains an embedded NUL at byte 20. Vulnerable `flexbuffers::Builder::StringOffsetCompare::operator()` uses `strncmp(..., min(len) + 1)` on these length-delimited strings, so the second string is treated as a duplicate of the first. `Builder::String()` then reuses the first string's offset but leaves the second string's 2-byte width in the pending `Value`, causing the serialized second vector element to point at a 1-byte-width string while advertising `byte_width_ = 2`. Later `GenerateText()` prints the nested flexbuffer, `Reference::ToString()` reads a bogus oversized length from the wrong-size prefix, and `EscapeString()` overreads one byte past the 1024-byte heap buffer. The staged patch fixes this by replacing the comparator with length-delimited `memcmp` plus a length tie-break, preventing the false duplicate and stale-width mismatch.

source.description: Source. The first `flex` array string from the attacker-controlled nested FlexBuffer value is materialized into the sharing-enabled `flexbuffers::Builder`, creating the string-pool entry later matched by the longer second string.
source.value_from: After `LLVMFuzzerTestOneInput()` strips the two leading flag bytes `0x20 0x20`, the remaining 303-byte body is `{flex:[...],name:""}` with no embedded NULs, so `parser.ParseJson()` sees the entire body. Byte 0 sets `opts.allow_non_utf8`, allowing the raw `0x87/0xff` bytes inside the string literals. The first `flex` element consumed here parses to 20 bytes; the second element, consumed later on the same parser path, starts with those same 20 bytes and parses to 256 bytes with `\u0000` becoming an embedded NUL at offset 20.

relation.description: Source identity relation for the vulnerability-relevant value.

sink.description: ASan crash site. `EscapeString()` iterates over an oversized length read from the malformed second string reference and performs the saved one-byte read past the end of the 1024-byte heap buffer.
sink.note: Stage 01's saved ASan report shows `READ of size 1` at this statement, 0 bytes to the right of a 1024-byte region allocated for the FlatBufferBuilder buffer while `Parser::ParseTable()` aligned the nested flexbuffer vector.

root_cause.description: Root cause. The string-sharing comparator applies C-string semantics to length-delimited FlexBuffers strings, so a longer string containing an embedded NUL at the shorter string's endpoint is treated as the same pool key.
root_cause.note: The staged patch replaces this with `memcmp(..., min_len + 1)` plus a length tie-break (`a.second < b.second`), matching length-delimited string ordering and preventing the false duplicate that leaves a stale width attached to a reused offset.

tainted_value_origin.description: Immediate origin of the second `flex` string. For the staged witness this second parsed value is 256 bytes long, begins with the first string's 20-byte prefix, and contains an embedded NUL at byte 20, so it is the value whose width/offset pair becomes inconsistent after duplicate reuse.
tainted_value_origin.value_from: The staged witness body contains two top-level `flex` strings. Reading the raw file bytes shows the first string literal occupies 20 bytes, while the second decodes to 256 bytes after interpreting its single `\u0000` escape as NUL; `WidthU(256)` therefore requires a 2-byte FlexBuffers string width.

parser_admitted.condition: For field `flex` from `tests/monster_test.fbs`, this branch is taken, so the JSON value is parsed by a fresh `flexbuffers::Builder(1024, flexbuffers::BUILDER_FLAG_SHARE_ALL)` and string sharing is enabled on the vulnerable path.

printer_dispatch.description: The saved crash stack reaches this nested-flexbuffer printer path, so `GenerateText()` reconstructs the serialized `flex` bytes as a FlexBuffers root and calls `root.ToString()` on them.

fine_trace.note: Source step. While parsing the nested `flex` array, this first string literal materializes the attacker's first FlexBuffers string into project state. For the staged witness it parses to 20 bytes and becomes the initial pool candidate that later collisions are matched against.

The first 20-byte string is serialized into the builder buffer and inserted into `string_pool`. `CreateBlob()` computes `bit_width = WidthU(len)`, so this pooled entry uses the 1-byte string width required for length 20.

The second attacker-controlled string is then serialized and prepared for duplicate lookup. For the staged witness it starts with the first string's full 20-byte prefix, has an embedded NUL at byte 20 (`\u0000` in the raw input), and parses to 256 bytes, so `CreateBlob()` gives it the 2-byte width required for length 256 before the pool lookup runs.

Root-cause step. The comparison length is 21 bytes here, so `strncmp()` stops when it sees the first string's terminator and the second string's embedded NUL at the same 21st byte. That makes the distinct 20-byte and 256-byte strings compare equivalent for `string_pool.find()`.

Because step 4 reported a false duplicate, the just-serialized 256-byte string is discarded and the current value is repointed at the first string's offset. Only `u_` is rewritten here; the value keeps the 2-byte `min_bit_width_` created for the 256-byte string.

When the vector is finished, the second string reference is encoded from the mutated `Value` created in step 5. Because non-inline strings use `min_bit_width_` as their stored width, the serialized packed type records a 2-byte-width FBT_STRING even though `u_` now points at the first string's 1-byte-width data.

During `GenerateText()`, the nested FlexBuffer vector is unpacked element by element. For the corrupted second element, the packed-type constructor on the returned `Reference` decodes the serialized packed type from step 6 back into `byte_width_ = 2` while preserving the reused offset.

The malformed second `Reference` is converted back into a `String` using `byte_width_ = 2`. `String` length retrieval reads `ReadUInt64(data_ - byte_width_, byte_width_)`, so this step interprets two bytes before the first string data as its length even though the pointed-to string was stored with a 1-byte prefix, yielding an inflated `str.length()`.

Sink. `EscapeString()` trusts the oversized `str.length()` from step 8 and keeps reading until `i == length - 1`; on the crashing run that takes `s[i]` one byte past the 1024-byte builder buffer, matching the saved ASan heap-buffer-overflow read at the right edge of `[0x619000000580, 0x619000000980)`.

allocation_context.note: AddressSanitizer reports that the crashing read lands 0 bytes to the right of a 1024-byte region allocated here while `Parser::ParseTable()` called `FlatBufferBuilder::ForceVectorAlignment()` for the nested `flex` field.

format.name: 305-byte monster_fuzzer corpus input
format.contract: Exactly the staged 305-byte input with SHA-256 `df455ccf78b0998fec62190c761eb8e25090700d40c4d275c1cce7016b788ca2`. The first two bytes are `0x20 0x20`; `LLVMFuzzerTestOneInput()` treats byte 0 as parser flags, enabling `opts.allow_non_utf8`, discards byte 1, and then passes the remaining 303-byte body to `Parser::ParseJson()` as `{flex:[...],name:""}`. In this witness the first parsed `flex` string is 20 bytes long, the second parsed `flex` string is 256 bytes long, the second begins with the first string's entire 20-byte prefix, and the second contains an embedded NUL at byte 20 via `\u0000`. Those exact properties are the verified trigger: they make `StringOffsetCompare` treat the strings as duplicates, leave the later 2-byte width attached to the earlier 1-byte-width offset, and cause `EscapeString` to read past the serialized nested-FlexBuffer heap buffer when `GenerateText()` prints the `flex` field. This GT does not generalize beyond this exact witness because the saved artifacts only prove this concrete 20-byte/256-byte string pair under `allow_non_utf8`.
